sheet.name: Brunhilde Stonehearth
sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. Keep the backstory true: Father Dorrin raised her long ago and she carries his book; nothing about it is recent or lost.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.

Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 2: 10 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

The mountain roads of the hill country are old dwarf-cut routes, and they carry more grief than trade these days. Rain loosens the slopes, and the small shrines along them are the only mercy for many miles.

Brunhilde Stonehearth, called Brun, grew up in one of those shrines. Father Dorrin Ashbeard found her as a half-starved child in a collapsed mine shaft and raised her in the Morninglord's light. His prayer book now rides in her pack, and she has come down from the hills to carry his blessing to those who need it.

Late afternoon, cold rain hammering the slate roof of the crossroads waystation. You have barely shaken the water from your braid when a roar of sliding stone tears across the pass. Beyond the inn's yard, a fresh rockslide has swallowed part of the road. Under it, muffled tapping and a thin voice calling for help: a wagon's worth of travelers, a wounded merchant, a child, a mule-driver.

At the edge of the rubble three strangers are already shouting. A nervous caravan guard wants to dig now. A sullen hunter, arms folded, says the slope above is still groaning and will bury them all. The innkeeper, wringing a rag, keeps looking from one to the other. Then all three turn to you, the cleric in the dented mail.

Above the rubble, small stones still trickle down. The tapping goes on beneath.

What does Brun do?

Brun steps up between the guard and the hunter, hands raised, and says calmly, "Nobody digs yet, and nobody stands around either. Hunter, you know this slope: where is it loose, and where will it hold? Guard, keep your people back until we have a plan." Then she kneels at the rubble, cups her hands to the stones, and calls down in a steady voice, "Hold on, we're coming. Tap once if you can hear me, and tell me who's hurt!"

Your hands find the rhythm of it, the same one Father Dorrin taught you in a hundred small chores: lift, test, set aside. Reading the rubble is not Stonecunning's trade, since that knows how stone was made, not how it will fall, but you have lived under fallen rock and your eyes learn fast. You spot the keystone slab holding the pile together and have the guard leave it alone, working around it instead. The innkeeper wedges planks beneath the overhanging edge as you go, and each time the hunter cries "Hold!" everyone freezes, and a heartbeat later a trickle of grit slides harmlessly past.

Half an hour of grim labor, and a gap opens at last: a dark hole just wide enough for a child, and beyond it the tilted bed of a wagon, water running along its floor. A small, muddy face peers out at you. "You came," Pip whispers.

Behind her, Tam the driver is bracing a beam with his shoulder, grey-faced. Further in, Ilsa lies pinned from the knee down under a fallen cask-rack and a heap of stone, her lips pale and her breathing shallow.

The gap is too narrow for the pinned woman, and the wagon still creaks. Pip could be passed out first, but Ilsa needs healing and lifting. What does Brun do?

Brun smiles at Pip and says, "Hello, brave one. Come out to me nice and slow, and the guard will take you somewhere dry." She hands Pip through to the guard, then calls to the hunter, "Keep watch on that slope, and shout if it so much as sighs."

Then she wriggles into the gap as far as her shoulders allow, reaches Ilsa, and speaks Healing Word to steady her, "Stay with me, Ilsa, you're not done yet." She tells Tam, "Once she's awake and breathing steady, you and I lever that rack up together while the guard drags her clear, and the innkeeper keeps the planks tight."

The path climbs steep and slick behind the waystation, switchbacking through wet bracken and shale. Garrick moves like a shadow; you move like a dwarf in chain mail, which is to say loudly, though you place each foot where his has been. You are watching your footing and the mist rolling off the ridge, and your thoughts are half on Ilsa's leg and half on Father Dorrin's old words about not letting haste make a second grave.

Near the top the old cairn stands stark against the grey, a heap of mossy stones taller than you. Garrick raises a hand, and you stop.

"There," he breathes.

Behind a screen of fallen rock, one that looks too neatly stacked to be natural, a dark opening yawns in the hillside, four feet wide and braced with fresh timbers, the pale square-cut wood bright against the old stone. Cold air breathes out of it, smelling of wet clay and lamp oil. Scattered at the mouth are boot prints, many, and a loose heap of spoil that has plainly come from inside. A pick with a broken handle lies beside it.

Garrick crouches and traces one print. "Last night. Maybe two or three of them. Still fresh." He glances toward the hole, then back at you, his hand on his bowstring. "I'll go no further without you saying so."

The tunnel is silent, and the drizzle ticks on the stone. What does Brun do?

Brun crouches beside the prints and keeps her voice low. "Garrick, stay at my shoulder with your bow ready. I'm going to cast Shield of Faith on myself before we step inside, and I'd like a closer look at those timbers and the broken pick first. If anyone's still down there, I'd rather talk than fight, but we go slowly and quietly, and if I raise my hand we stop."

A shimmering field settles over you like a breath of warm light, and the damp chill slides off your armor. Garrick glances at it, says nothing, and nocks an arrow.

You run a thumb along the nearest prop and then turn the broken pick in your hands, and your eyes catch what a hurried glance would miss. Burned into the pale wood, small and neat on the underside of the timber and again on the haft of the pick, is a brand: a hammer over three wavy lines.

You know it. Every dwarf child in the hills does. It is the mark of the old mine-wardens of Hearthdeep, the hold whose galleries run under the very hills where you were found as a child. The wardens' stores were sealed when the lower mines fell in, and no new timber should bear that brand. Yet this wood is days old, cut and shored to a warden's exacting standard. Whoever is digging here has the wardens' tools, their stock, or their knowledge, and the proper dwarven way of shoring means the diggers expect to dig long and deep. And since those timbers are set carefully, whoever placed them did not mean for the hill to fall. The slide was something else going wrong.

Cold air still breathes from the opening, smelling of wet clay and lamp oil. Your Shield of Faith will hold for about ten minutes if your concentration does. Garrick waits at your shoulder, bow ready.

What does Brun do?

Brun runs her thumb over the brand once more and murmurs, "Hearthdeep wardens... that's the hold under the hills where Father Dorrin found me. Garrick, remember this mark; somebody's using a dead hold's name, or its stores." She lifts her shield and steps to the opening, whispering, "Slow and quiet, I'll lead with the shield since it's holding. Keep your arrow ready, and stay a few paces behind me."

She calls softly into the dark first, in Dwarvish, "Friends from the road, hold your tools. I'm a healer of the Morninglord and I mean no harm. Is anyone hurt down there?"

Your Dwarvish rolls into the dark, and for a long moment nothing answers but dripping water. Then, from perhaps thirty feet down the tunnel, a lamp shutter clicks open and a crossbow bolt whispers past your ear and thunks into a timber at the opening, a hand's breadth from your head. A warning, and a good shot, since the shot was meant to miss.

"That's far enough, surface-walker," a woman's voice growls in the old tongue, roughened by dust and cold. "Healer of the Morninglord, are you? Plenty come with kind words. Who's the man with the bow behind you?"

In the lamp's thin glow you make out a squat figure braced behind a timber, a dwarf with a grey-shot beard braided in the wardens' fashion, a second crossbow cocked and ready. Others shift in the dark behind her, at least two more by the sound. Their lamps are shuttered, but you hear a cough, wet and ragged, from further in.

"Say your piece quick," the woman says. "I have no mind to kill a priest, but I'll not let this hole be taken from us."

Garrick's breathing is steady behind you, his arrow still drawn. Your shield glimmers in the lamplight, its blessing about five minutes from fading.

What does Brun say or do?

Brun keeps her shield low and her hands open, speaking in Dwarvish. "My name is Brun Stonehearth, raised by Father Dorrin Ashbeard at a shrine near Hearthdeep. The man behind me is Garrick Thorne, a hunter, and he'll lower his bow if you'll lower yours. Garrick, easy now, and let the arrow down."

She says to the dark, "I heard a cough that sounds wet and bad, and healing is the only thing I came to offer. Who is hurt, and what is it you're guarding down here? Your slide buried a wagon yesterday, and I pulled a child out of it, so I think we both have things to say."

Silence stretches. Behind you Garrick lowers his bow an inch at a time, jaw tight. In the dark the crossbow does not waver, but the voice, when it comes, has lost a little of its edge.

"Ashbeard." She says it as if tasting it. "The old priest of the hill shrine. He buried my brother's wife, once. So you're his foundling." A pause. "Doesn't mean I trust you, girl. Fine words come cheap. But hear this: we did not bring that slope down. The seam gave from above, not below, and it took one of ours with it. We've been three days trying to shore what's left."

The cough comes again, deeper, wet, and someone mutters a curse.

"Here's my terms. You come in alone, no hammer in your hand. Leave it at the mouth. Your hunter stays out in the rain with his bow lowered, and if I hear one string drawn, you'll be the first I put a bolt in. You can look at Aldric. Then we talk."

Garrick's eyes meet yours, uneasy. "I don't like it," he says low. "But it's your call, dwarf."

Your Shield of Faith will fade in a few minutes. The tunnel beyond is narrow, timbered, and dark, with several armed dwarves in it, and a sick one who may need you. What does Brun do?

Brun sets her warhammer carefully against the cairn side of the opening and says to Garrick, "Stay here and keep your bow down, my friend. If I'm not out within the hour, go back and tell the innkeeper what we found, and don't come after me alone."

She raises her empty hands and calls into the dark in Dwarvish, "Thank you, Hild, my hammer's at the mouth and I'm coming in slowly, with only my holy symbol and my healing. Show me Aldric."

Your hammer leans against the cairn, and Garrick's face goes flat with worry. Then the dark takes you. The blessing around you fades like a candle guttering, and the tunnel closes in, low, cold, and shored with the wardens' brand every few paces. The tools and lamps along the walls are old stock, kept well.

Just before the first bend someone hisses from the shadows, "Hild, she's coming in with nothing in her hands." You take the name with you.

At the bend a lamp opens, and Hild Ironvein steps into the light, a squat, grey-braided dwarf with a crossbow trained on your chest and dust ground into every line of her face. Two more dwarves hover behind her, a younger man with a pick in a white-knuckled grip and a one-eyed woman holding a lantern. None of them lower their weapons.

"Aldric's through here," Hild says. "Mind your head, and mind your hands."

A side gallery opens to the left, hung with canvas against the draught. On a pallet of sacks lies a stocky dwarf with a bandaged chest and a grey, sweat-slicked face, each breath a wet rasp. Dried blood stains his lips. His eyes find you and widen. "A priest," he whispers. "Hild... you brought a priest."

Beyond him, deeper in the gallery, the lamplight touches something that is not rock: a smooth, curved surface of old stone set into the wall, and a great iron-banded door half-cleared of clay.

You have one spell slot, and the dwarf is badly hurt. Hild's crossbow has not moved. What does Brun do?

Brun kneels beside Aldric without a glance at the crossbow and says gently in Dwarvish, "I'm here, Aldric. Don't talk, just breathe slowly for me." She lays her hand on his wrist and listens to his chest, checking the bandage and the color of his lips with her Medicine training.

"Hild, I'll need one lamp brought close and some clean water, and I'd like to know how he was hurt and how long ago. If it's what I fear, the lung is filling, and I'll cast Cure Wounds on him now."

The one-eyed woman sets a lamp and a basin of water beside you without a word. Hild lowers her crossbow, not far, only to her hip.

"Yesterday, when the seam gave," she says, grudging but answering. "A beam took him across the ribs. And before you ask, the cough's older than that. Started three days ago, the same as Dunna's and the boy's." The young man with the pick looks away.

You lay your palm on Aldric's chest and pray, and the Morninglord's warmth runs through your hand. The broken ribs ease and the bruising pales; his breath deepens and his eyes clear. You listen again, though, and it is not enough. Beneath the crush there is another sound, a crackling wet rasp deep in the lungs that does not come from the beam. You read the injury only halfway, and the other half of it you cannot name.

"Better," Aldric breathes. "Gods, better." Then the cough takes him again and he spits something grey into the cloth. Hild's mouth thins.

"It's the air," says the one-eyed woman quietly, her gaze sliding toward the end of the gallery. "It comes off the door. Sweet-smelling when the wind turns, and then you cough." She says nothing more.

Hild watches you, and for the first time something other than suspicion is in her face: fear, tightly held. Your spells are spent, and the iron door breathes cold at the gallery's end.

What does Brun do?

Brun sits back on her heels and says quietly in Dwarvish, "Hild, the beam was only half of it. The rest is in the air, and I'd bet my life it's coming from that door. Everyone who's coughing needs to be moved back toward the mouth of the tunnel and into the open, right now, with Aldric carried on his pallet."

She looks to the one-eyed woman. "You noticed the sweet smell. Has anyone gone near the door, and has anyone worked closest to it? Ask them to keep a wet cloth over their nose and mouth until we're out, and I'll look at the door from a distance once everyone's breathing fresh air."

input.add_to_description: Crew: Aldric (hurt), Dunna (one-eyed woman, coughing), and a young man with a pick (also coughing). Motive revealed after Brun moved everyone out: the lower Hearthdeep galleries were sealed after a collapse about forty winters ago that trapped many of the hold's dead; Hild's kin among them. The crew dug in to bring them out for proper burial. The warden stores and timber were taken from the sealed upper stores.

Hild looks at you for a long breath, and then at the cloth Aldric spat into. "Dunna," she says to the one-eyed woman, "the door's yours to answer for. Boy, wet your scarf and take the pallet's head. Move."

There are no more words. The crew lifts Aldric between them and carries him back through the shored gallery, cloth over every mouth. Dunna answers you as she goes, in a low rasp: it was her and the boy who worked nearest the door, mostly in the last three days, chipping clay from the seams. Sweet-smelling air, cold as a cellar, a taste like old pennies on the tongue. The more they dug, the worse the cough. Nobody had gone through; the door had never opened.

You come out into grey daylight and thin rain, and the open air is a shock of sweetness after the tunnel. Garrick is on his feet at once, bow half raised, and you wave him down with a word. He stares at the dwarves, at Aldric on his pallet, then at you, and slowly lowers the arrow.

Aldric drags in a deep, clean breath and then another, and the color eases in his face. Dunna sags against the cairn, coughing, then straightens.

Hild stands apart, rain running down her braids, and says nothing for a while. When she speaks, her voice is lower. "Forty winters back, the lower galleries of Hearthdeep fell with half the hold's miners in them. The wardens sealed what they couldn't reach and set a door on it. Our kin are still down there, my brother among them. We came to bring them out for proper burial, so they might rest in the earth as they should." She looks at you hard. "We didn't pull that slope down. And we never meant to bring anything out but our dead."

You have no spells left, and the tunnel breathes its foul air in the hill behind you. A wagon party's life has been saved, a crew's life is in your care, and a door waits. What does Brun do?

Brun lays a hand on Hild's arm and says gently in Dwarvish, "Then you have my word, Hild: I'll help you bring your kin out, and I won't let anyone else use that door either. But not today, and not until the air is understood, because I owe you the truth: whatever breathes off it is making your people sick, and Father Dorrin taught me never to let haste dig a second grave."

She turns to Garrick. "Would you take Aldric, Dunna and the boy down to the waystation on a cart with the innkeeper's help? I'll keep watch here with Hild, pray for my spells at dusk, and then we go back in with wet cloths and a plan."

Hild stares at your hand on her arm, then at your face. Some of the iron goes out of her shoulders. "Haste dug the first grave," she says, half to herself. "Aye. Forty winters of it." She nods once, a short, hard thing. "Your word, then. I'll hold you to it, Stonehearth."

Garrick says little, as ever, but he is already moving. He and the innkeeper's cart, fetched from the waystation at a trot by a boy sent running, carry Aldric, Dunna and the young man down the cairn path wrapped in blankets and breathing clean air. Garrick's parting look says plainly that he thinks you are mad, and a half-nod says he would not leave you out here alone anyway. He promises to bring a hot meal and Ilsa's news by midday.

By nine the mouth of the tunnel stands quiet in the drizzle. Hild sits on a flat stone at the cairn, crossbow across her knees, watching the black opening. The rest of her crew are gone, all but a lean grey-bearded dwarf you haven't met, Corm, who has been keeping the fire and now sets a pot over it without a word.

One thing needs saying, since you will not be able to pray your spells back by dusk: you finished a long rest only hours ago, and the rules of rest allow only one in a day, so your magic will not return until about four tomorrow morning. Until then you have only your hammer, your Sacred Flame, Guidance, and your wits.

The door still breathes behind the hill. Hild waits for your plan.

Brun nods at Hild and takes the seat beside her. "Then we use today to learn, not to dig, Hild. Tell me everything the wardens left: any marks, records, or sealing words on that door, and whether your family kept a map of the lower galleries." 

She adds, "And Corm, if that stew has room in it, I'll gladly take a bowl. DM: just to be sure, I still have Pip's tin bell on my belt and my warhammer is still leaning at the tunnel mouth, correct?"

time: 1 hour later: Day 2, 10:05 AM

Yes on both: Pip's tin bell still hangs at your belt, and your warhammer still leans where you left it against the cairn side of the opening. Hild grunts when you stand to fetch it, and does not stop you.

Corm ladles a thick bowl of stew, barley and salt pork, and presses it into your hands without a word. It is the best meal you have had in days.

Hild digs a folded square of waxed cloth from inside her coat. Within is a charcoal rubbing of the iron door's marks and a half-torn map of the lower galleries, copied from some warden's ledger her family kept. You study both for the better part of an hour, tracing the lines with a finger. The workmanship is unmistakably the wardens', hold-cut stone fitted without mortar, and by the weathering it is some forty winters old. But you cannot make the center of the door speak. A three-stroke sign repeats across its face, and it might mean bury, or might mean keep shut, and the difference matters very much. On the half-map, one gallery is marked with a hammer split in two, and you cannot tell what that means either.

Across the fire, Corm has stopped stirring. He is staring at the rubbing in your hands, and for a moment his face goes the color of ash. When he sees you looking, he turns back to the pot.

"Old marks," Hild mutters. "Corm was apprenticed to the wardens as a boy. Won't say much."

The rain has thinned to a mist, and the day is still young. You have a rubbing, a half-map, an unsaid answer, and no magic. What does Brun do?

Brun sets her bowl down, carries the rubbing over to Corm, and crouches beside him, keeping her voice soft. "Corm, I saw your face when you looked at this. You don't have to say it all, but that three-stroke sign and the split hammer on the map: do they mean 'bury' or 'keep shut'? Whatever it is, I'd rather hear it from you than learn it by opening that door."

She adds, "Nobody here is going to think less of you for a hard memory. Father Dorrin used to say a truth shared at a fire weighs half as much."

Corm does not look up. His thumb travels to the inside of his left forearm, where beneath the rolled sleeve a pale, puckered scar runs in the shape of a hammer, and it rests there. For a moment you think he will answer. Then he shuts his eyes.

"Leave it be, Stonehearth," he says, hoarse, in Dwarvish. "You've a good heart. Don't ask me that. Not at the fire, not today." He rises, takes his bow and a coil of snare-wire, and goes up the ridge without another word.

Hild watches him go, mouth tight. "He's been like that since we found the door," she says. "He'll speak when he's ready or he won't. I've learned not to push a dwarf who's carrying a grave."

The morning drags on. You make a careful copy of the rubbing in your prayer book's margin, mark the split hammer on the map, and take stock of the tunnel: foul air still breathes at its mouth, so you keep well clear.

A little after noon, Garrick comes up the path with a basket of bread and cold mutton, a flask of broth, and news. Aldric, Dunna and the boy are resting at the waystation with the innkeeper's wife, coughing less in the clean air. Pip is under Ilsa's bed teaching the mule driver a rhyme. Then Garrick sets the basket down and rubs his neck.

"The merchant's awake and wants you. Alone, she says. Says her cargo's not what her manifest says, and she'll not tell a soul but the dwarf who set her leg."

Hild's eyes narrow. The tunnel breathes behind you, and Corm's silence hangs on the ridge. What does Brun do?

Brun accepts the bread and mutton, then says to Hild, "I'll go hear what Ilsa has to say and be back before dusk. Please keep everyone away from that tunnel mouth, and if Corm returns, let him be; I'll not push him again." She turns to Garrick. "Lead the way, friend, and tell me on the path if the innkeeper's wife needs anything for Aldric's cough."

Garrick leads you down the cairn path, and on the way tells you that the innkeeper's wife has the three coughers on steam and honey and willow-bark, which she says is as much as anyone could do for lungs. At the waystation the yard is half-cleared, planks and shovels leaning against the wall, the wagon's wreck still lying at the road's edge under tarps. Inside, the common room smells of broth and peat smoke. Pip waves from the hearth with a spoon, and Tam the driver nods you toward the back room.

Ilsa sits propped on pillows with her splinted leg raised, color good, eyes sharp. She waits until Garrick has closed the door.

"You set my bone twice and never asked what I carried," she says. "So I'll tell you, because I think it killed that slope." She pulls a folded paper from under the blanket: her manifest, all lamp oil, salt, and bolts of wool. "Under the oil barrels, in a false bottom, there's a chest. Lead-lined, iron-bound, no bigger than a bread box. A stranger paid me triple to leave it at the old cairn above this station, and said someone would collect it. Hooded, a dwarf, grey-bearded, spoke Common with a hill accent. He wore gloves, but when he handed me the coin his sleeve rode up and I saw a scar on his forearm like a hammer."

She swallows. "The chest has the wardens' brand burned into the lid. At night it's warm, Brun, like a living thing, and I swear it hums. The slide came the moment we got close to the cairn path. I don't know what's inside it, and I don't want to. But it's still in the wreck."

Beyond the door, Pip's laugh rings, and the rain starts again against the shutters. What does Brun do?

Brun holds Ilsa's hand and says quietly, "Thank you for trusting me with this, Ilsa. That scar matches the one Corm showed me at the fire, so I think he knows far more than he's said, and we'll be careful with him, not cruel." 

She turns to Garrick. "Nobody touches that chest, and nobody lets Pip or the mule near the wreck. Can you and I look at the wagon from a distance, with Tam keeping the yard clear, and I'll tell you what I think before anyone lifts a finger?"

You take your leave of Ilsa with a squeeze of her hand, then go out into the rain with Garrick. Tam, set to keep the yard clear, herds the innkeeper's boy and Pip indoors with a loud tale about a dragon in the kitchen.

From forty feet you study the wreck under its tarps. The wagon bed has slumped, its false-bottomed barrels split, and through the gap, half-hidden in sodden straw, you can see a squat iron-bound box. You see more. The tarp above it does not run with rain the way the rest does. It steams, a thin pale vapor lifting from the canvas as if the lid beneath were warm. Frost has bloomed on the iron bands, although the air is merely cold and wet. When the wind drops, you feel a low hum behind your teeth, the same pitch Garrick winces at and touches his jaw for.

And you see something Garrick does not. Where the cairn path meets the road, a thin line of grit and pebbles has been trickling across the mud toward the wreck all afternoon, uphill to down, in a slow, patient thread, as if the hill itself were leaning toward the chest.

"I don't like it," Garrick mutters. "Not one bit. Rock doesn't do that."

Your hammer is in your hand. Your spells are gone until near dawn, and the chest sits in the rain like a held breath. What does Brun say or do?

Brun keeps her eyes on the thread of pebbles and says low, "Garrick, I don't think the hill is leaning toward the chest by chance. Let's not touch it or pull it away yet, but I want that yard and the road kept clear, and a rope line staked around the wreck at forty feet so nobody wanders close, especially Pip."

She adds, "Then I'll send word up to Hild: the chest is down here, and whoever left it, the scarred dwarf, may be Corm's kin or Corm himself. Can you fetch the innkeeper and have him tell the other guests to sleep upstairs tonight, away from that side of the building?"

time: 5 hours 30 minutes later: Day 2, 7:05 PM

Garrick does not argue. He takes one more long look at the thread of pebbles and starts working. By midafternoon the wreck is ringed with stakes and a rope at forty feet, hung with the innkeeper's old cowbells so that anything crossing it will be heard. Tam and the guard take the yard in shifts. The innkeeper moves the guests upstairs without fuss, Pip and the three coughers at the far end of the hall, Ilsa carried up on her plank door. Garrick sends the innkeeper's boy up the cairn path with your message for Hild: the chest is below, the scarred stranger may be Corm or his kin, watch the tunnel and stay out of it.

The day wears away into a cold, wet dusk, and the hum has not stopped. You feel it now in your breastbone when you stand near the window. The thread of grit has thickened into a slow stream.

A little past seven, a bell clinks on the rope line, once, softly. You are at the door in a moment, hammer in hand, Garrick a step behind with an arrow nocked.

A lean figure stands at the edge of the lamplight, hooded, cloaked in oiled wool, just short of the rope. He is breathing hard, as though he has run all the way down the ridge in the dark. He does not look at you. He is staring at the steaming tarp, and the frost on the iron bands, and his face under the hood is the grey of old ash.

It is Corm. He holds his bare left forearm out into the light, scar and all, and says in Dwarvish, hoarse and broken: "I paid the merchant. I put it in that wagon. And I think I have killed us all."

The hum in your teeth deepens. What does Brun do?

Brun lowers her hammer at once and steps out to the rope, keeping her voice level and kind. "Corm, I'm here and I'm listening, and nobody is going to strike you. Stay on your side of the rope, breathe with me, and tell me plainly: what is in that chest, and what did you hope to do with it?"

She adds quietly over her shoulder, "Garrick, ease the arrow down, but keep it close."

input.add_to_description: Corm's confession (Day 2 dusk): the chest holds the warden's keystone-seal, the 'heartstone' that bound the Iron-Banded Door forty winters ago. Corm, a warden's apprentice, was sworn to keep it; he took it from the door three nights before the slide because he feared Hild's crew would break through and release what the wardens sealed in the lower galleries (a sleeping thing that fouls the air; the 'split hammer' on the map marks its gallery). He meant to hide it in the old warden ward-cairn far from the door but could not carry it far (it burns his scarred arm), so he paid a courier. Removing it weakened the seal: the air seeps, the hill leans toward the stone, the slide followed. The stone wants to return to the door; the longer it is away, the weaker the seal.

time: 25 minutes later: Day 2, 7:30 PM

Corm sags against a fence post, and the words come out of him as if he has carried them forty winters.

"It is not a burial, girl. Not bound by grief. The three strokes mean bound, not buried. The lower galleries didn't fall by themselves. Something woke in the deep, a sleeper the miners broke into, and it fouled the air and the stone and the men who breathed it. The wardens sealed it in. Sixty souls, and the hold's own dead among them, so the rest could live." His hand trembles on the scar. "I was fourteen. My master gave me the heartstone to keep when he walked in through the door and let them shut it behind him. That chest is the heartstone. It's what holds the door."

He swallows. "When Hild's crew came digging, I knew they would break through. I took the stone away three nights past, meaning to carry it far, to the old ward-cairn on the other side of the hill where the wardens' dead lie and the rock is clean. But it burns my arm, and I'm old. So I paid the merchant, and swore to meet her at the cairn. And the hill... the hill wants it back. It's been dragging toward the door ever since I moved it. The slide was that. Without the stone the seal fails a little more each hour. That's why they cough."

He looks at you with eyes that are all grief. "I don't know whether to put it back or carry it away. If I put it back, Hild digs through and wakes it. If I don't, it wakes anyway."

The hum in your breastbone deepens, and from the dark the bell on the rope line clinks again, though no one has touched it. Overhead, the wind has the sound of a long, slow breath. It is not yet night, and your spells are hours away.

What does Brun say or do?

Brun steps up to Corm and puts a steadying hand on his shoulder. "Thank you for telling me, Corm. That was a heavy thing to carry alone for forty winters, and you don't carry it alone now."

"Here's what I think, and tell me if I'm wrong: the stone must go back before the seal fails any further, because carrying it away just lets whatever is below wake with nothing holding it. Then Hild needs to hear all of this from your own mouth, and she must promise me she'll never dig that door open. I gave her my word to help bring her kin home, and I'll keep it, but not at the price of that thing waking."

She turns to Garrick. "Can you wake Tam and the guard, and help me wrap the chest in wet canvas and lift it with the long planks, never touching it with bare hands? Corm, you know the stone best, so you tell us how to carry it and how to set it back."

Corm lifts his head, and something like relief crosses the ruin of his face. "Wet canvas, double thick," he says. "Iron tools, not bare hands. Never let it touch the earth between here and the door. It knows the way back; it will pull toward the hill, so keep it level."

Garrick wakes Tam and the guard, and the innkeeper brings canvas and two long planks from the woodpile. Soaked in the trough, the canvas hisses and steams where it meets the lid. You and Garrick lift on the planks, Tam and the guard take the far ends, and Corm walks ahead with a lantern, murmuring warden-words under his breath that you almost recognize from Father Dorrin's old prayers. The chest comes up out of the straw, impossibly heavy, as if the stone inside were sinking through the earth.

The climb is a black, wet hour. Under the hum the path seems to move, and in the dark and rain you lose the line Garrick walked this morning and stray onto the clay-wet side. Your boot skids, the plank slews, and the iron band cracks painfully across your shield arm. You hold. Corm swears and has the chest back level before it can touch the ground. You bleed a little and bruise, but the stone stays off the earth, and the canvas holds.

You reach the tunnel mouth at nine, soaked and shaking. Hild stands in the lamplight with a lantern in one hand and the crossbow in the other, Aldric's empty pallet behind her. She sees Corm, then the chest, and her face closes like a fist.

"Corm," she says, very softly. "What did you do?"

Behind her the tunnel breathes. The hum fills the air, and the iron door waits at its end. You are at 10 hit points, with no spells until near four. What does Brun do?

Brun steps between Hild and Corm, keeping her hands open and her voice steady. "Hild, lower the crossbow and hear him out, because he's been carrying this for forty winters and it's why your people are coughing. Corm, tell her what you told me, all of it, the three strokes, the sixty souls, and your master at the door."

She glances at the chest, held level on its planks. "Garrick, Tam, keep it off the ground a little longer. Hild, I gave you my word to bring your kin home, and I'll keep it, but first I need yours: nobody opens that door until we have set the stone back and understand what's behind it."

time: 20 minutes later: Day 2, 9:20 PM

For a long moment no one moves. Rain taps on the planks and hisses on the steaming canvas. Hild's crossbow stays level at Corm's heart, and Corm does not flinch from it.

Then he tells it. Slowly, in the old tongue, the three strokes, the sixty souls, the boy of fourteen with the heartstone in his hands and his master's back disappearing into the dark as the door swung shut. Hild's jaw works. When he reaches the part about her brother, the miners' names read out one by one by the wardens before the sealing, hers among them, the crossbow dips.

"My brother Brenn," she says, hoarse. "He's down there. You're telling me he's not dead the way the dead are dead."

"He's bound," Corm whispers. "Like all of them. Whatever walks in the deep wears the dead as well as the living, Hild. If you open that door, you won't bring Brenn home. You'll bring home what has his face."

Her breath shudders out of her. She looks at you then, and the grief in her face is something you have seen only in mirrors. "You said no digging till you understood," she says. "You said you'd never let haste dig a second grave." Her voice cracks. "Then say it plain, priest. You give me your word you'll find a way to honor him. And I give you mine: nobody opens that door."

She lowers the crossbow entirely. Behind her the lantern flickers, and the hum swells until the planks tremble in your hands.

The chest wants to go in. The iron door waits at the gallery's end, and you are tired, bruised, and out of spells. What does Brun do?

Brun meets Hild's eyes and says softly, "You have my word, Hild: I'll find a way to honor Brenn and every name on that list, with prayers said over them properly, and not one grave dug by haste. Thank you."

Then to the others, "Corm, lead us in, wet cloths over every face, iron tools only, and tell us at each step what to do. Garrick, Tam, keep the chest level and off the earth, and if anyone feels the hum in their chest turn bad or the air go sweet, say so and we stop and back out."

She shifts her shield arm, wincing, and takes up the rear plank. "Slow and together, and I'll keep my hammer ready but not drawn."

Brun, the stone has settled and you have earned your second level. Here is the story first, and then the choice.

The tunnel closes around you as you walk, Corm leading, wet cloths over every mouth. At the iron door the hum rises until your teeth ache. Corm sets the planks on the iron tool-rest and speaks the warden's words, a flat, rough chant, and your Wisdom holds against the sweet, sleepy pull that rises when the canvas is peeled back. You hold it, just barely, steadied by Father Dorrin's old prayers. You speak your binding prayer beside Corm and reach for the words and cannot quite grasp them whole.

The stone seats in the door's heart with a deep, grinding note. The hum drops to a low, even breath, like a sleeper turning over and settling. But the seal is only half-mended: the lines on the door still gleam too faintly, and the air still smells a little sweet. It will hold, for now, with a warden's hand upon it.

Corm lays his scarred arm against the iron and says quietly, "My master stayed. I was a boy and I ran. I'll not run again." Hild sits down on the cold floor beside him, crossbow across her knees, and says nothing. Brenn's name lies unspoken between you.

You have completed the rescue and more. You are at 300 XP and may take level 2 now.

Level 2 gives you:
- Hit points: take the fixed 9 more HP, or roll 1d8 and add your Constitution +3 (plus 1 for Dwarven Toughness, at least 1 total before it).
- Channel Divinity, once per rest, with two options: Turn Undead, and Preserve Life (heal up to 10 HP, divided among creatures within 30 feet, no more than half their maximum).
- A third first-level spell slot, and you can prepare 5 spells instead of 4 after a long rest.

Do you take the fixed 9 hit points or roll the d8?
I'll take the fixed 9 hit points, steady and sure. And for my fifth prepared spell I'd like Protection from Evil and Good, given what sleeps behind that door.

Your voice is low and even in the cold gallery. The old evening prayers come easily, in Father Dorrin's cramped phrasing, and when you reach the end you say Brenn's name once, plainly, and then the names of the sixty that Corm can give you, one at a time. Hild's lips move silently with the first. Corm keeps his scarred arm against the iron and does not lift his head, but his shoulders ease.

Somewhere in the reading, the hum in your teeth fades to nothing. The door breathes slow and even, like a sleeper, and the sweet smell thins. One by one your companions doze against the wall, and you, with your shield for a pillow and your hammer within reach, follow them down.

The night passes without trouble. You wake near six, stiff and warm, with grey light creeping down the tunnel from the mouth. Your wounds are mended and your spells restored: you are at 21 hit points, with all three first-level slots, Channel Divinity ready, and Protection from Evil and Good prepared beside Healing Word, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary and Shield of Faith.

Corm has not moved from the door. His face is lined but calmer than you have seen it. "The seal holds," he says without turning. "It will not do so forever. A true binding needs the old rite, and that needs a warden's ledger, or a priest of your Morninglord who knows the words of sealing. Father Dorrin may have left some of it in that book of yours. RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

You climb a few steps and call up the stair. Corm's voice answers, thin and steady: the seal has stirred twice in the hour but settled both times, and he is well. When it ends, you have rolled one hit die: 8 plus 3 for 11 hit points, which takes you back to 21 of 21 with nothing to spare, so you keep the second die. Channel Divinity is ready again. Your spell slots are still spent. A short rest does not return them, and they come back only with a long rest, the next one possible around six tomorrow morning.

Yes, exactly: 21 of 21, one hit die left, Channel Divinity ready, and no spell slots until a long rest.

You go in slowly, lamp low, shield up, and Hild a pace behind, eyes on the ceiling. Your sweep turns up two old rat nests in rotted sacking, long abandoned, and a rusted snare-wire strung across the aisle at ankle height, the wardens' crude alarm, tripped long ago and left slack. You step over it and point it out to Hild, who spits and steps over it too. Nothing else stirs.

At the lectern the ledgers lie in a rack of dry slate, their covers tough as old boot leather. Hild and you turn them one by one under the lamp, and then your hand falls on one without knowing why: the warden-captain's own, its last leaf marked by a strip of faded blue ribbon. Inside, in a tight, upright Dwarvish script, is the Naming.

You read it twice. It is shorter than you feared, a litany of the sixty names, a plea, and a closing word of leave-taking. Beside it the captain has written more than the rite needs. The sleeper below is no monster. It is a hurt and grieving thing, the mountain's own stone-spirit, woken when the lower seam was cut, and the wardens bound it out of fear. The Naming can bind it again, as Corm believes, but it can also release it, if the keeper consents and the sixty are named aloud.

One name is marked in a different hand. *Brenn Ironvein, volunteer. Walked in of his own will to keep it company, and to hold its hand.* You read it to Hild, who goes very still, and then very quiet, and then covers her face with her sleeve.

The rite must be spoken at dawn, by a priest of the Morninglord, at the door, with the keeper's hand upon the stone. That is dawn tomorrow, about six. It is a little before nine now.

What does Brun do?

Brun lays a hand on Hild's shoulder and waits until the dwarf lowers her sleeve. "Hild, Brenn wasn't taken, he chose to stay, and chose to keep something frightened company. Whatever else is true, that's a kind thing, and we'll honor it."

She tucks the captain's ledger into her pack wrapped in a dry cloth. "Let's carry this up to Corm now, and read the rite through together with Hild and him before dawn. Corm has to hear what the captain wrote about releasing it, because it's his hand on the stone and it's his choice to make, not mine."

Hild drops her sleeve and looks at you for a long moment, her eyes red-rimmed and fierce. "Chose to stay," she says. "That's Brenn. He always did pick the lonely end of a rope." She laughs once, a cracked sound, and wipes her eyes with the back of her hand. "Aye. We'll honor it."

You wrap the ledger in dry cloth and tuck it into your pack beside Father Dorrin's book. The two of you climb back past the first bend with your lamp low and the rats' droppings crunching under your boots.

Corm is where you left him, his palm flat on the iron, his scarred arm pale in the lamplight. He listens in silence while you read the Naming aloud, and then the captain's closing note: that the sleeper may be bound, or may be released, if the keeper consents and the sixty are named. When you read Brenn's line he closes his eyes.

"My master wrote none of this," he says at last. "He told me only to keep it shut." He is quiet for a long time. "I have spent forty winters afraid of a thing that was afraid." He lowers his head. "Give me the day, Stonehearth. It is my hand, as you say, and it is a heavy choice. At dusk I will tell you which."

Hild sits down beside him. Neither speaks again.

It is a little after nine, with nearly a day to dawn. Your spell slots return only with a long rest, which you can begin tonight and finish near dawn. You have a ledger, a rite, and a dwarf's decision to wait for.

What does Brun do with the day?

Brun nods and says, "Take all the time you need, Corm. Whichever you choose, I'll stand beside you, and I'll not press you again." She sets her pack down and adds, "Hild, I'd like to go down to the waystation for a few hours, check on Aldric, Dunna and Ilsa, and tell Garrick and the innkeeper that the door holds and nobody is to come up the cairn path. I'll bring back hot food for you both and be here again before dusk."

On the way, she'll copy the names of the sixty into the back of Father Dorrin's book so she can speak them clearly at dawn.

Garrick carries the basket and neither of you says much on the way up. The rain has thinned to a fine mist and the hillside is quiet, only a wren somewhere in the bracken. At the tunnel mouth Hild is waiting on her flat stone, and she gets up to meet the hunter. They look each other over like two cats in a yard, then Hild nods and takes the basket without a word. Garrick sets his bow across his knees on the rock beside the opening, plainly settled for the night.

In the gallery below, the three of you eat in the lamplight, bread and stew and cheese, and for a little while it is almost cheerful. Corm barely touches his. When the last bowl is scraped, he lays his spoon down and wipes his hands on his knees.

"I have decided," he says. His voice is steady for the first time since you met him. "I'll not bind it again. I was a boy, and I was told to keep it shut, and I have kept it shut for forty winters, and it has been afraid every one of them." He looks at the iron door. "I will put my hand on the stone, as the keeper must. You will say the names, Stonehearth. You will say Brenn's last. And when it is done and the door is open, if it opens, I will go down with Hild and bring up what we can bury."

Hild nods once, hard. "I'll stand beside him."

"It may go badly," Corm adds. "It may wake angry. A keeper's hand does not always protect the keeper."

Outside the mist darkens into night. You have the ledger, the names copied in your book, and one night before dawn. Your spells return only with a long rest, which should begin soon if you are to be ready.

What does Brun do?

Brun puts a hand over Corm's scarred one and says quietly, "Then I'll stand with you, and I'll say every name as if it were my own family's. If it wakes angry, I'll have Sanctuary and Protection from Evil and Good ready for the three of us, and I'll not leave your side."

She turns to Hild. "Let's all sleep in turns tonight, with Garrick keeping the outer watch, so I can take my long rest and have my spells by dawn. And before I lie down, I'll read the names through once more aloud, so they're steady in my mouth."

You take your hands from Corm's, and say the names aloud once through: the sixty, one at a time, in the captain's tight order, with Brenn's last. You say them again, softer, until they sit steady in your mouth like beads on a cord. Then you lie down on your blanket by the wall with your shield for a pillow, and Hild takes the first watch, her crossbow across her knees.

The night passes. Twice you half wake to the soft sound of Garrick's boots on the stair and the murmur of his report to Hild: all quiet, nothing on the path. Once you hear the stone's slow breath at the end of the gallery, like a sleeper who has begun to dream. Corm never sleeps.

You wake a little before six, and the grey light is already in the tunnel mouth. The long rest has done its work: you are at 21 of 21 hit points, with all three first-level slots and Channel Divinity ready. You still have Healing Word, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, Shield of Faith and Protection from Evil and Good prepared, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready besides.

Corm is standing at the door with his scarred arm already bared and his palm laid flat against the iron beside the heartstone. He does not turn. Hild stands at his shoulder, her crossbow lowered and slung. Garrick has come down from the mouth and waits at the bend with his bow unstrung, because Corm asked him to. The air is cold and still, with nothing sweet in it, and the hum has gone so quiet you can barely feel it in your teeth.

"Dawn," Corm says. "Whenever you're ready, Stonehearth."

Brun steps up to the door beside Corm, opens Father Dorrin's prayer book to the captain's rite, and sets her holy symbol against the cold iron. Before she begins, she casts Protection from Evil and Good on Corm, since his hand is the one on the stone, and says softly, "Steady, old friend. I'm here."

Then she begins the Naming in a low, clear voice, saying the Morninglord's invocation first, and then each of the sixty names slowly, one at a time, with Brenn Ironvein's last.

The ward settles over Corm like a held breath, and his shoulders ease a hair. You open Father Dorrin's book, set your holy symbol against the cold iron beside his scarred hand, and begin.

The Morninglord's invocation first, a low, plain line of light. Then the names. One by one, in the captain's tight order, each given room to be heard. By the tenth the hum under your feet has changed pitch; by the thirtieth the iron beneath your palm is warm. Somewhere deep in the hill, something turns over and listens.

It does not wake gently. At the forty-first name the door shudders, dust sheets down from the lintel, and a vast, slow, sorrowing voice rolls up through the stone, not words but the memory of words, the sound of a weight on a heart. It is afraid. Your whole body knows it. And it is angry in the way the frightened are.

You hear what it asks. It is not release it wants, not at first. It wants *them to stay*. It has been so long alone. You catch your voice before it breaks, and your Wisdom holds. You say the next name, and the next, and you do not stop, because Father Dorrin once found a starving child in the dark and did not stop either.

At the last name you lay your forehead against the iron. "Brenn Ironvein," you say. "He held your hand. You may let go now. We have come to hold it for him."

The light stands up out of your holy symbol, soft gold, like a sunrise through a doorway, and fills the gallery to the vault. Hild falls to her knees. Corm's hand does not move. The great door groans and swings inward on a breath of cold, clean air, with no sweetness in it at all.

Below, as far as the lamplight carries, a long dark gallery opens, and in it, in rows, still and peaceful, the sixty lie in their places, as if sleeping. The voice in the stone is quiet. A sigh, then silence, then nothing but the slow drip of ordinary water.

When it is done, Hild's crew are on their feet and weeping. Garrick has taken off his hood. They are calling you something in Dwarvish, softly, a name that will follow you: the *Lantern of Hearthdeep*.

You earned 250 XP, now 600 of 900. The seal is mended, the dead can come home, and the rest of the day belongs to burying them. What does Brun do?

Brun wipes her eyes, closes Father Dorrin's book, and says softly, "Then let's bring them home properly, Hild. Corm, would you lead us down, and Garrick, could you fetch the innkeeper and the folk at the waystation to help carry and dig?"

She kneels at the first of the sixty and begins the Morninglord's burial prayer, and when she reaches the place where a name is wanted, she looks to Hild. "Show me where Brenn lies, and we'll bring him up first."

Corm takes the lamp and leads, and you walk down into Hearthdeep together with Hild at your shoulder. The galleries are dry and cold, with nothing bad in the air. The sixty lie where they were bound, their tools beside them, their faces calm. There is no rot, only a long, quiet stillness, as if the mountain kept them as a promise.

Hild finds Brenn at the lowest gallery's head, sitting against the wall with one hand open on his knee, exactly as the ledger said. She kneels and does not speak, and then she lays her forehead on his hand. You say the burial prayer over him first, as you said you would, and then you move down the rows, one after another, with the name each time.

By midmorning the whole waystation is on the hill. Garrick has brought the innkeeper and his wife, Tam and the guard, Aldric on a stick, Dunna and Tobin with their cloths over their mouths for old habit, and Pip, in the arms of Ilsa's carriage-boy, solemn with a cairn-stone clutched in her fist. They carry the sixty out on planks and doors, and dig sixty graves in clean earth by the old ward-cairn, each marked with a cairn-stone and a name. Corm digs his master's grave himself and will not be helped.

You say the prayers at each one. By noon your voice is rough as gravel and your arms ache, and the last stone is set. Hild's face is wet and she is smiling for the first time since you met her. She sets a hand on your shoulder. "You'll have a place at any hearth of Hearthdeep," she says. "Whatever remains of us."

Pip tugs at your sleeve. The bell at your belt chimes once, softly, as if on its own. You ring it for her, the way you promised, and she laughs.

The rockslide is cleared, the road is open, and the hold is quiet. It is a little past noon, and you have 600 of 900 XP, with 2 of 3 spell slots and a ledger that is now Corm's to keep. She turns to Hild and Corm. "Before I go anywhere, I'd like to say goodbye properly. Would you tell me what you know of the Deepwatch, and would you walk with me to Father Dorrin's shrine once more, to pray there before I set out?"

You turn the prayer book over in your hands, and its worn spine feels strange now, as if it held a door you had never opened.

I will be plain about what the story knows. Nothing in your past says Father Dorrin ever spoke of the Deepwatch to you, and the note itself is the only mention. What your mother's people were is yours to say. The note is his hand and his word, and I will not write your family for you.

Hild answers first, wiping her face with her sleeve. "The Deepwatch? Aye. Every warden's child knows the name. It is the old mother-hall of the mine-wardens, up in the high hills north of here, three days' walk if the passes are clear. Where they keep copies of every hold's ledgers, and the names of the lost." She considers you. "Folk say a warden's kin are still sworn there, whatever became of the holds. If your mother's people were of the wardens, that is where they'd be recorded."

Corm has been standing a little apart, his scarred arm bare in the afternoon light. He nods slowly. "Hold-kin go there to ask. I never did. I was afraid of what they would say about what I did." He looks at you. "Take the captain's ledger, if you want it. It is a copy of one at the Deepwatch. They will want to see you with it. I will not need it now."

At the cairn the wind lifts, and the two of them walk with you a little way up the slope to where the road runs into the hills toward the old shrine, as you asked, though it is a long road home and you will pray there at dusk. The bell at your belt chimes once as you walk, and the hills lie wide and grey and open before you.

You are at 21 of 21 with 2 spell slots left, 20 gold, and 600 XP of the 900 for third level. The road north to the Deepwatch is three days, the road back to the shrine is shorter, and the waystation is below.

What does Brun do?

Brun accepts the ledger with both hands. "Thank you, Corm. I'll carry it to them with care, and with your name on it."

"I'll pray at Father Dorrin's shrine first and tidy it for whoever comes next. Then I'll go north to the Deepwatch. Hild, if you hear anything of the wardens' kin, send word to the waystation, and Garrick will know where to find me." She turns toward the shrine road, the bell chiming at her belt. "DM: just to check, how much gold do I have now, and is Pip's bell still on my belt?"

You have 20 gold pieces, the five from Ilsa's purse added to your fifteen, and yes, Pip's tin bell still hangs at your belt, chiming softly as you walk.

Behind you the cairn field sits quiet under the grey sky, sixty stones in a clean row. Ahead the road bends toward the old shrine, then the high hills and the Deepwatch beyond.

You have a long road before you and a few ways to take it. You could ask Garrick to come, as he half-offered, or go alone. You could stop first at the waystation for supplies, or head straight for Father Dorrin's shrine.

What does Brun do?

Brun stops and turns to him with a warm smile. "Garrick, I'd be glad of your company and your knowledge of the passes. Come with me to the waystation first so we can fill our packs, and say goodbye to Pip and Ilsa properly."

time: 1 hour later: Day 4, 1:49:30 PM

Garrick stops in the road and looks at you for a long moment, as if checking the weight of the offer. Then he gives one short nod. "I'll fetch my pack," he says, and for the first time since you met him there is the ghost of a smile under the hood.

He is your companion now. The hunter has his longbow, a shortsword at his hip, and a leather coat oiled against the rain. He is a second-level ranger, familiar with these high passes and wise to monsters of the mountains. He has two ranger spells too, Hunter's Mark and Cure Wounds, and two slots to cast them from.

At the waystation the yard is quiet in the afternoon light. The wagon wreck has been cleared from the road, and a patched cart waits at the stable door, where Tam and the mule are already loading it. The innkeeper's wife gives you a sack of oatcakes and dried apple, which you take with thanks, and Ilsa, propped on her chair at the door, presses a wool scarf into your hands against the cold of the passes. Pip stands at the foot of the steps, chin high, trying very hard not to cry.

You ring the little tin bell once, and she takes it in both hands, the way you promised, and holds it to her ear. "It rings at the end of the story," she says. "So you have to come back."

"I will," you say.

It is nearly two in the afternoon. Father Dorrin's shrine lies a half day's walk the other way, and the road north goes up into the high hills from here.

What does Brun do?

Brun kneels to Pip and tucks the bell gently into her small hands. "Keep it safe for me, Pip, and ring it whenever you miss me. I promise I'll come back and tell you the end of the story."

She stands, shoulders her pack, and nods to Garrick. "Shrine first, then. We'll walk until dusk and camp wherever the road gives us shelter, and I'll cast Shield of Faith or Sanctuary if anything troubles us on the way."

Pip's fingers close around the bell, and she holds it against her chest as if it might escape. "I'll ring it every night," she says fiercely. The bell is hers now, so it is gone from your belt and your pack, and you feel the lightness of it.

You and Garrick take the road west under a clearing sky. He walks a little ahead, eyes on the ridgeline, saying nothing, and the quiet is a comfortable one. The road climbs, drops into a gully of birch and wet bracken, and climbs again. You eat oatcakes on the move.

The light is going gold and low when the shrine comes into view on its shelf of rock: a small, squat stone hut with a slate roof, a lean-to for travelers, a stone Morninglord's sun carved over the door, exactly as you left it. Smoke does not rise from it. There is no one to light the fire.

Garrick, scanning the slope as you approach, misses the thing at the door, and you almost do too. Someone has been here since you left. The shrine's door stands ajar, a fresh mud-print of a boot lies across the step, and a small pile of stones has been built on the threshold, three in a row: the wardens' sign for *kin passed here*.

Within, a candle burns on the altar, lit not long ago, with its wax still soft.

Your pack is heavy, the light is failing, and Garrick has unslung his bow without a word. You have two spell slots and Channel Divinity. What does Brun do?

Brun lifts a hand to stop Garrick, then speaks low. "Easy, friend. Whoever left that sign meant kin, not harm, and I'd like to be the first through the door, with my hammer down and my holy symbol showing."

She steps onto the threshold, nudges the door wider, and calls softly in Dwarvish, "This is Brun Stonehearth, Father Dorrin's foundling. If you lit that candle, I'm home, and I mean no harm."

time: 10 minutes later: Day 4, 6:29:30 PM

Your voice goes into the little stone room and comes back to you from the walls, the way it did through all your childhood evenings. For a moment there is only the candle's small sound.

Then something stirs near the altar, and a figure rises slowly from the bench where the old priest used to sit. A dwarf woman, ancient even by dwarf reckoning, her braids white as bone and bound with iron rings, a worn warden's cloak pinned at the shoulder with a hammer-and-three-lines brooch. She leans on a staff of black oak. Her eyes are your eyes: soot-dark, steady.

She says, in the old tongue, hoarse with the road, "I told myself I would sit one hour and go if you did not come. It has been three days." She looks at you the way you looked at the names in the ledger. "You have his chin. Your mother had that same stubborn chin, Brunhilde."

You cannot move. Garrick's bow lowers by itself behind you.

"My name is Maren Stonehearth," she says. "I am your mother's mother's sister, and the last of the wardens' line that sat at the Deepwatch before the holds fell. Dorrin wrote to us the winter you came to him. We could not come. We were told a child was found in a collapsed shaft, and that she would be safer where no warden's blood was known." Her voice thins. "That was a lie told to keep us frightened. I have regretted believing it every year since."

On the altar beside the candle lies a small, battered iron ring, braided with a lock of auburn hair gone dull with age, the same auburn as your own.

"It was hers," Maren says. "I carried it three days to put it in your hand. The Deepwatch has news of Hearthdeep, and of you. Whether you come north is your choice. But tonight I would like to sit in a warm place with my kin, if you will have me."

The shrine is quiet. The candle gutters and steadies. The ring lies on the altar, waiting.

What does Brun do?

Brun crosses the little room in three strides, and when she reaches the altar her hand trembles over the iron ring before she closes her fingers around it. "Aunt Maren," she says, her voice breaking on the word, "yes. Please sit. I'll light the hearth and put the kettle on, and Garrick will help me, because tonight this is a warm place and you are kin."

She slips the ring onto her smallest finger and turns back, wiping her eyes. "I have so many questions, but first tell me one thing: what was my mother's name, and how did she die?"

Maren sits down on the old priest's bench and does not answer until the fire is lit. Garrick splits kindling with his shortsword, you set the kettle on the hook, and the little stone room fills slowly with warmth and the smell of woodsmoke. It is the first fire the shrine has had since you left.

Then she tells you.

"Sigrun," she says. "Sigrun Stonehearth. A warden-surveyor, the best the Deepwatch ever sent down a shaft. She could read a seam like you read a face. She drew the maps the hill-holds still use." She almost smiles. "Stubborn as an anvil. She would not be told a shaft was unsafe if her own line said otherwise."

The fire pops. Maren's hands tighten on her staff.

"The shaft she was surveying outside the hold gave way while you were with her. She was not meant to have you there; the nurse had fallen ill, and she would not leave you alone. When the roof came down she put herself over you. That is how you lived. They dug for four days. Dorrin found you on the fourth, alive under her, cold, and holding a handful of her braid in your fist."

She nods at the ring on your finger. "That is what he cut from it. He kept it for you, and then, I think, he did not know how to give it. He wrote to us once, and we did not come, and the years went on."

Her eyes are wet but her voice does not break. "As for your father, he was not a warden. The rest is in the Deepwatch records, and it is not mine to say by a fire at night, half told. Come north, and I will show you the page."

Garrick keeps his eyes on the flames and says nothing, but when you glance at him he has set a second cup beside Maren's, and filled it, and nudged it toward you. Outside the stars are coming out over the hills.

You are home, at the shrine where Father Dorrin raised you, with kin at the fire and a ring on your finger. It is a little past eight. You have two spell slots, Channel Divinity, and a long road north when you are ready. What does Brun do?

Brun takes the cup Garrick set for her, holds it in both hands, and sits down beside Maren, leaning her shoulder against her aunt's. "Thank you, Aunt Maren. I'll come north, and we'll read that page together when I'm ready."

"But tonight I'd like to stay here and keep Father Dorrin's hearth lit one last time, and say the evening prayers aloud with you, if you'll join me. Garrick, you'll share the watch with me?" She smiles, a little wet-eyed, and adds, "DM: just to be sure, I still have Corm's ledger and Father Dorrin's prayer book in my pack, correct?"

Yes: Corm's ledger and Father Dorrin's prayer book are both in your pack, wrapped in dry cloth, and the ring is on your smallest finger.

You say the evening prayers aloud with Maren, the old priest's words in two voices, hers dry and cracked, yours low and steady. When you reach the place where Father Dorrin's name belongs, you say it, and she says it after you. The hearth burns down to a bed of red. Garrick takes the first watch at the door with his bow across his knees, and you take the second. Nothing comes up the road. Once in the small hours an owl asks its question and no one answers.

You sleep in the old priest's own bed, on the old priest's own blanket, and for the first time in a long while you do not dream of stone.

It is a little after four in the morning when you wake, rested, at 21 of 21 hit points with all three spell slots and Channel Divinity ready. The same five spells are prepared, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready besides. Grey light is just starting in the shrine's one window. Maren is already up, sitting by the cold hearth with her staff across her knees, watching you with an expression you have not seen on anyone's face before, one you suspect is called pride.

Garrick has the packs ready by the door, and the road north runs up into the high hills, three days to the Deepwatch.

What does Brun do?

Brun rises, folds Father Dorrin's blanket neatly on the bed, and lays a hand on the lintel of the little shrine for a moment before she shoulders her pack. "Aunt Maren, Garrick, I'm ready. Let's be on the road north while the light is still gray and the passes are quiet."

She stirs the cold ashes once and says softly, "Rest well, Father. I'll come back and tell you how it ends."

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Deepwatch Lead

The road north climbs out of the birch gullies and into bare, wind-scoured hills, where the grass lies flat and the cairns of old warden waymarks stand at every rise. You leave the shrine's smoke behind you at the first ridge and do not look back, though you want to. Maren walks slower than you, her black staff striking the stones in an even beat, but she does not falter and she does not complain.

Garrick takes the lead and reads the land like a page. Where the old track washes out at a stream, he finds the ford; where it climbs into scree, he finds the sheep trail that skirts it. Twice he stops, lifts a hand, and listens, then goes on. Nothing follows you. Once a pair of ravens wheel overhead for an hour, and Maren says they are only ravens.

By midafternoon you have crossed two ridges and a high saddle, and Garrick estimates you are a full day ahead of the pace he feared. "The Deepwatch is two days yet," he says, not turning his head. "Maybe a day and a half, if the weather holds. There's a warden's waymark-hut at the next saddle. We can shelter there tonight."

It is half past two. The sky is high and pale, the wind steady, and the path ahead runs on through the hills, long and bare and quiet. You are at full strength, with three spell slots and Channel Divinity ready, and kin walking beside you.

What does Brun do?

Brun falls into step beside Maren and shortens her stride to match. "Aunt Maren, while we walk, would you tell me about the Deepwatch itself, and about my mother as a girl? I'd like to hear the small things, like what she liked to eat and what songs she sang."

She glances ahead at Garrick and adds, "Garrick, thank you for the ford and the sheep trail. At the waymark-hut tonight I'll cook, since you've done the hard work all day."
